name: Pore vacuum

lead: A pore vacuum is a small electric suction tool pressed against the skin to draw blackheads and surface oil out of pores, aiming for a clearer, smoother-looking nose and cheeks.

The device creates suction at a nozzle placed against the skin, with the intent of drawing keratin and sebum out of open comedones. No published clinical trials of these consumer devices were found, so the evidence for their effect is limited to manufacturer claims and user reports. Dermatology references describe manual extraction and retinoids as established approaches to comedones.

paras: Users typically steam or warm-wash the face first, then glide the nozzle over the skin for short passes, and follow with a cleanser or toner. It is a consumer gadget sold online and in stores.
General guidance on extraction notes risks of irritation, bruising, infection and scarring from skin trauma. No safety studies of consumer suction devices were found.

angle.text: Pore vacuums use suction to pull sebum plugs out of pores, so there are fewer visible blackheads and skin looks clearer. They are popular consumer gadgets, and no clinical trials were found.

lead: A pore vacuum, also sold as a blackhead vacuum or suction blackhead remover, is a handheld electric device that applies suction through a small nozzle held against the skin. Manufacturers market it for drawing sebum and keratin plugs, commonly called blackheads, out of facial pores.

Blackheads are open comedones: hair follicles blocked by keratin and oil, with a dark surface that results from oxidation rather than dirt [1]. Dermatology references describe manual comedo extractors, used with careful hygiene after steaming or warm washing, and retinoids and azelaic acid as treatments for comedones [1]. Suction devices are not described in that reference.

No published clinical trial of consumer pore vacuums was identified for this article. Evidence for the category therefore rests on manufacturer claims and user reports rather than on controlled studies.
infobox: Typically rechargeable electric, with interchangeable nozzles

paras: Consumer pore vacuums are small electric units with a vacuum pump and a set of nozzle heads of different shapes and openings. Many models offer several suction levels. The user presses the nozzle against the skin, usually the nose and cheeks, and moves it across the area.

Comedones form when keratin and sebum block a follicle. An open comedone is a blackhead and a closed one is a whitehead. Contributing factors listed in medical references include increased oil production, genetics, greasy hair products and ingrown hairs, and over-washing or scrubbing may irritate skin [1].

Reference sources note that dermatologists can often remove open comedones with minimal trauma, while closed ones are harder to extract, and that squeezing or picking can cause infection or scarring [1]. Pore-cleansing strips are described there as potentially damaging to skin [1].

No safety studies of consumer pore vacuums were found. General dermatology guidance on extraction warns that trauma to skin can lead to infection and scarring [1]. Users on consumer review sites and forums commonly describe redness, temporary marks or bruising when suction is applied too long or too strongly, but these are anecdotal reports and were not cited here.
